text.en: Anu and Kabir were playing in the park when they saw Geeta Aunty step out of a taxi. She is a pilot in the Indian Air Force, the pride of the town. Another neighbour, a retired Border Security Force man, now grows vegetables and teaches computer skills to young people on weekends. Everyone around us does so many things every day. Which of these are work for pay, and which are done out of love or duty? In this chapter we learn the value of all kinds of work.

Activities that people do can be divided into two groups: economic activities and non-economic activities. Economic activities are those done to earn money or to produce goods and services that are exchanged, such as a pilot flying for a salary, a farmer selling vegetables or a teacher paid a monthly salary. Non-economic activities are done without expecting money: parents cooking for the family, children helping with homework, youth caring for grandparents, neighbours helping to repair a house or a volunteer teaching without a fee. Some people do both. Geeta Aunty serves the country and gets a regular monthly salary, which is an economic activity. A retired soldier who also volunteers teaches for free, which is a non-economic activity.
A market is a place where people exchange goods and services. Goods are things we can touch, such as rice and chairs. Services are help provided by people, such as a doctor's treatment or a driver's trip. People may exchange goods and services for other goods and services, but in most cases they use money.
A salary is a regular payment, usually monthly, from an employer. A fee is paid for professional advice or services, as to a doctor or lawyer. Payment in cash is in money. Payment in kind is a non-cash payment: in Kavya's aunt's village a worker on the orchard gets part of the payment in cash and the rest in mangoes of equal value. Wages are paid per day or per task, such as to a construction worker operating an excavator on the new highway.
Economic activities add value at each stage as something is changed into another form. A carpenter buys wood for Rs 600 and makes a chair that sells for Rs 1,000. The extra Rs 400 pays for his skill, time and effort. He has added value. Roads, hospitals, schools and shops all add value to our lives.
Non-economic activities do not earn money but have great value. Langars or community kitchens at gurudwaras feed every visitor free, and temples distribute prasad. Community participation is another strong value. The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan depends on the efforts of all citizens to keep surroundings clean, and Van Mahotsav, the festival of forests, spreads awareness about trees. Such work builds bonds, saves resources and creates the caring society in which economic activity can flourish. All honest work deserves dignity.

problem.en: Classify each activity as economic or non-economic: a tailor stitching clothes for pay; a child watering plants at home; a bus driver; a neighbour who helps an elder cross the road.

text.en: A tailor stitching for pay is economic.
Watering plants at home and helping an elder are non-economic.
A bus driver earns wages, so it is economic.

problem.en: A farmer buys seeds for Rs 2,000, grows vegetables and sells them for Rs 5,500. How much value did the farm work add?

text.en: Selling price minus buying price: 5,500 minus 2,000.
So Rs 3,500 of value was added by the work and effort.

prompt.en: Why are non-economic activities valuable even though they bring no money?

requiredIdeas.en: They build values like care and cooperation.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking only paid work has value.

points.en: Work is of two kinds: economic and non-economic.
People are paid by salary, fee, wages, in cash or in kind.
Work adds value to materials and to life.
Non-economic work and community participation have great value.
